knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines the objective class, oracle-access model, and objective-gap accuracy criterion.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given $L>0$ and $n\in\mathbb N$, consider $\min_{x\in\mathbb R^n}f(x)$ with $f\in\mathcal F_L^{\infty,1}(\mathbb R^n)$, accessed through a local first-order black-box oracle. knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a smooth convex objective on Euclidean space accessed through a local first-order black-box oracle, an epsilon-approximate solution has objective value at most epsilon above the infimum.

knowledge_statements.title: Unconstrained Smooth Objective Model
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional deterministic minimization with globally Lipschitz gradient.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(f:\mathbb{R}^d	o\mathbb{R}\) be continuously differentiable. The unconstrained \(L\)-smooth objective model is
\[\min_{x\in\mathbb{R}^d} f(x),\qquad \|
abla f(x)-
abla f(y)\|\le L\|x-y\|\quad	ext{for all }x,y\in\mathbb{R}^d,\]
where \(L>0\). A solution is any \(x^\star\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in\mathbb{R}^d}f(x)\), when this set is nonempty. Without convexity, the basic first-order target is instead an \(\varepsilon\)-stationary point satisfying \(\|
abla f(x)\|\le\varepsilon\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Minimize a differentiable function over Euclidean space using a globally Lipschitz gradient; solutions are global minimizers, while nonconvex analysis commonly targets small gradient norm.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\min_{x\in\mathbb{R}^d}f(x)\) is the unconstrained smooth model, with \(\|\nabla f(x)-\nabla f(y)\|\le L\|x-y\|\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Unconstrained smooth convex optimality and minimizing sequences
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Combines the smooth convex problem model and minimizing-sequence terminology with the convex first-order optimality characterization; the latter is cross-indexed to convex analysis.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f:\operatorname{dom}f\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}\) be convex and twice continuously differentiable on its open domain, and suppose its infimum is attained. Write \(p^\star=\inf_x f(x)\). For every \(\bar x\in\operatorname{dom}f\), \[\bar x\in\operatorname*{argmin}_x f(x)\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad \nabla f(\bar x)=0.\] A sequence \(\{x^{(k)}\}_{k\ge0}\subseteq\operatorname{dom}f\) is a minimizing sequence if \(f(x^{(k)})\to p^\star\). For a prescribed tolerance \(\epsilon>0\), the stated termination test is \(f(x^{(k)})-p^\star\le\epsilon\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For an attained unconstrained problem with a twice continuously differentiable convex objective on an open domain, a domain point is optimal exactly when its gradient vanishes. A sequence is minimizing when its objective values converge to the optimal value. The stated stopping test requires an objective gap no greater than epsilon.
assumptions_latex: f:\operatorname{dom}f\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}\text{ is convex and twice continuously differentiable on its open domain}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \forall \bar x\in\operatorname{dom}f:\ \bar x\in\operatorname*{argmin}f\iff\nabla f(\bar x)=0;\quad f(x^{(k)})\to p^\star\text{ defines a minimizing sequence};\quad f(x^{(k)})-p^\star\le\epsilon\text{ is the stated termination test}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Unconstrained Smooth Minimization Problem
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Extraction-grounded definition of the finite-dimensional problem, its optimal points, and the attained optimal value when a minimizer exists.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Given \(f\in\mathcal F_L^{1,1}(\mathbb R^n)\), the unconstrained smooth minimization problem is
\[
\min_{x\in\mathbb R^n}f(x).
\]
Any \(x^*\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in\mathbb R^n}f(x)\) is an optimal point. When such a point exists, its attained value is denoted by \(f^*=f(x^*)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An unconstrained smooth minimization problem minimizes a function in the class F_L^{1,1} over all of R^n. Every global minimizer is an optimal point, and when a minimizer exists its attained objective value is denoted by f*.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: x^*\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in\mathbb R^n}f(x)\Longrightarrow x^*\text{ is optimal and }f^*=f(x^*)

knowledge_statements.statement_title: First-order local oracle and joint accuracy criterion
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Source-specific oracle-access and approximate-solution definitions for unconstrained smooth strongly convex minimization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix \(n\ge1\), \(\mu>0\), and \(L\ge\mu\). Consider \(\min_{x\in\mathbb R^n}f(x)\) with \(f\in\mathcal S^{\infty,1}_{\mu,L}(\mathbb R^n)\), and let \(x^*\) be its unique minimizer with \(f^*=f(x^*)\). A first-order local black-box oracle returns \((f(x),\nabla f(x))\) when queried at \(x\in\mathbb R^n\). For \(\epsilon>0\), a point \(\bar x\in\mathbb R^n\) is an approximate solution with accuracy \(\epsilon\) if \[f(\bar x)-f^*\le\epsilon\qquad\text{and}\qquad\|\bar x-x^*\|^2\le\epsilon.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For this unconstrained smooth strongly convex problem class, a local first-order oracle returns the objective value and gradient at each query. The source's ε-accuracy criterion requires both objective error at most ε and squared distance to the unique minimizer at most ε.
assumptions_latex: x^*\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in\mathbb R^n}f(x)\text{ is the unique minimizer}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \mathcal O_f(x)=(f(x),\nabla f(x));\qquad \bar x\text{ is an approximate solution with accuracy }\epsilon\iff f(\bar x)-f^*\le\epsilon\ \text{and}\ \|\bar x-x^*\|^2\le\epsilon.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Smooth Bounded-Below First-Order Problem Class
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A joint problem, oracle, and approximate-stationarity specification for unconstrained smooth minimization; convexity is not assumed.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The class $\mathcal G_*$ consists of problems $\min_{x\in\mathbb R^n}f(x)$ with $f\in C^{1,1}_L(\mathbb R^n)$ and a value $f^*\in\mathbb R$ satisfying $f(x)\ge f^*$ for every $x\in\mathbb R^n$. A first-order black-box oracle returns $(f(x),\nabla f(x))$ at each queried point. Relative to $x_0$, an $\varepsilon$-solution is a point $\bar x$ satisfying $f(\bar x)\le f(x_0)$ and $\|\nabla f(\bar x)\|\le\varepsilon$.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: This class contains unconstrained objectives with an L-Lipschitz gradient and a finite lower bound. Its oracle returns the objective and gradient, and an epsilon-solution must not increase the initial objective value and must have gradient norm at most epsilon.
assumptions_latex: \exists f^*\in\mathbb R\;\forall x\in\mathbb R^n:\ f(x)\ge f^*
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \bar x\text{ is an }\varepsilon\text{-solution}\iff f(\bar x)\le f(x_0)\ \text{and}\ \|\nabla f(\bar x)\|\le\varepsilon

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Unconstrained Smooth Convex Minimization Problem
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines the unconstrained problem for an L-smooth convex objective, including the strongly convex regime when \(\mu>0\), together with optimal solutions and the optimal value.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(n\in\mathbb N\), \(\mu\ge 0\), \(L>0\), and \(f\in\mathcal S^{1,1}_{\mu,L}(\mathbb R^n)\). The associated unconstrained problem is \[\min_{x\in\mathbb R^n}f(x).\] A point \(x^*\in\mathbb R^n\) is an optimal solution if \(f(x^*)\le f(x)\) for every \(x\in\mathbb R^n\). When such a point exists, the optimal value is \(f^*:=f(x^*)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For an L-smooth convex objective on Euclidean space, possibly strongly convex, the unconstrained problem minimizes the objective over the whole space. An optimal solution has value no greater than that at any other point, and this value is denoted by f*.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: x^*\text{ is optimal}\iff (\forall x\in\mathbb R^n)\ f(x^*)\le f(x),\qquad f^*:=f(x^*)\text{ when an optimizer exists}.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The unconstrained nonlinear optimization problem has the form

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(d\in\mathbb{N}\) and a differentiable objective \(f:\mathbb{R}^d\to\mathbb{R}\), the exact local first-order oracle is the mapping
\[\mathcal{O}_f:\mathbb{R}^d\to\mathbb{R}\times\mathbb{R}^d,\qquad \mathcal{O}_f(x)=\bigl(f(x),\nabla f(x)\bigr).\]
Given an initial query \(x_0\in\mathbb{R}^d\), a deterministic first-order method may, for each \(k\in\mathbb{N}_0\), generate
\[x_{k+1}=\Phi_k\bigl((x_0,\mathcal{O}_f(x_0)),\ldots,(x_k,\mathcal{O}_f(x_k))\bigr),\]
where \(\Phi_k:(\mathbb{R}^d\times\mathbb{R}\times\mathbb{R}^d)^{k+1}\to\mathbb{R}^d\) is a fixed update map. This oracle supplies the objective value and gradient at each queried point, but no Hessian or higher-order derivative information.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The exact local first-order oracle returns the objective value and gradient at a queried point. A deterministic first-order method chooses each subsequent query through a fixed map of the accumulated query-and-response history.

knowledge_statements.title: Quadratic Objective Models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Symmetric positive-semidefinite quadratics used to expose first-order spectral dynamics.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A convex quadratic objective model on \(\mathbb{R}^d\) has the form
\[f(x)=\tfrac12 x^{\mathsf T}Qx-b^{\mathsf T}x+c,\qquad Q=Q^{\mathsf T}\succeq0,\]
with gradient \(\nabla f(x)=Qx-b\). It is \(L\)-smooth when \(\lambda_{\max}(Q)\le L\), and it is \(\mu\)-strongly convex when \(Q\succeq\mu I\) for some \(\mu>0\). A minimizer exists exactly when \(b\in\operatorname{range}(Q)\), in which case every minimizer solves \(Qx^\star=b\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A convex quadratic is determined by a symmetric positive-semidefinite Hessian. Its extreme eigenvalues control smoothness and strong convexity, and minimizers solve the associated linear system.
assumptions_latex: \(Q\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times d}\) is symmetric and positive semidefinite.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\nabla f(x)=Qx-b\), with smoothness and curvature determined by the spectrum of \(Q\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Minimizer of an SPD Quadratic Model
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Closed-form minimization of a local quadratic model with a general symmetric positive-definite metric.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let G\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n} be symmetric positive definite and let f be differentiable at \bar{x}. For \phi_G(x)=f(\bar{x})+\langle\nabla f(\bar{x}),x-\bar{x}\rangle+\tfrac12\langle G(x-\bar{x}),x-\bar{x}\rangle, the unique minimizer is x_G^*=\bar{x}-G^{-1}\nabla f(\bar{x}).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A quadratic model whose curvature matrix is symmetric positive definite has the unique minimizer obtained by applying the inverse curvature matrix to the negative gradient at the base point.

knowledge_statements.title: Quadratic Momentum Stability
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Schur-stability condition for constant-parameter heavy-ball dynamics on positive-definite quadratics.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For the heavy-ball iteration
\[x_{k+1}=x_k-\alpha(Qx_k-b)+\beta(x_k-x_{k-1})\]
on a quadratic with \(Q\succ0\), the error in an eigendirection of eigenvalue \(\lambda\) obeys
\[z_{k+1}=(1+\beta-\alpha\lambda)z_k-\beta z_{k-1}.\]
This mode is asymptotically stable exactly when both roots of
\[r^2-(1+\beta-\alpha\lambda)r+\beta=0\]
lie in the open unit disk. For real parameters, the equivalent inequalities are \(|\beta|<1\), \(\alpha\lambda>0\), and \(\alpha\lambda<2(1+\beta)\). Stability on the entire spectrum requires these inequalities for every \(\lambda\in\operatorname{spec}(Q)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Heavy-ball stability reduces to a second-order scalar recurrence in each eigendirection. All characteristic roots must lie strictly inside the unit disk for every eigenvalue.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Quadratic momentum is stable exactly when \(|\beta|<1\), \(0<\alpha\lambda<2(1+\beta)\) for every \(\lambda\in\operatorname{spec}(Q)\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Descent Lemma
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Quadratic upper model for an L-smooth function on a convex subset of a Euclidean space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(D\) be a convex subset of a Euclidean space \(\mathbb E\), and let \(f:\mathbb E\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be \(L\)-smooth on \(D\), where \(L\geq0\). Then, for all \(x,y\in D\), \[f(y)\leq f(x)+\langle\nabla f(x),y-x\rangle+\frac{L}{2}\|x-y\|^2.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An L-smooth function on a convex set lies below its first-order approximation plus one half L times the squared distance between the two points.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Trial-point majorization condition used by backtracking line search.

source_refs.locator: 10.3 Analysis of the Proximal Gradient Method-The Nonconvex Case p. 272

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(d\in\mathbb{N}\), a differentiable function \(f:\mathbb{R}^d\to\mathbb{R}\), a base point \(x\in\mathbb{R}^d\), and a trial curvature \(M>0\), define
\[Q_M(y;x)=f(x)+\langle\nabla f(x),y-x\rangle+\frac{M}{2}\|y-x\|^2.\]
A trial point \(y\in\mathbb{R}^d\) satisfies the local quadratic upper-model condition when
\[f(y)\le Q_M(y;x).\]
If \(\nabla f\) is \(L_{x,y}\)-Lipschitz on a neighborhood of the segment joining \(x\) and \(y\), then the condition holds whenever \(M\ge L_{x,y}\). In gradient backtracking, one may test \(y_M=x-M^{-1}\nabla f(x)\) and increase \(M\) until the displayed condition holds. If \(\nabla f\) is Lipschitz on a fixed neighborhood of \(x\), then this procedure accepts for all sufficiently large \(M\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A local quadratic upper-model test compares the objective at a proposed point with a quadratic model based at the current point. A Lipschitz constant valid near the tested segment guarantees the test when the trial curvature is at least that constant; local Lipschitz continuity near the base point therefore ensures eventual acceptance by gradient backtracking.

knowledge_statements.title: Smooth Nonconvex Regime
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Smooth minimization without convexity, measured by first-order stationarity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The smooth nonconvex regime consists of objectives \(f:\mathbb{R}^d\to\mathbb{R}\) that are differentiable, bounded below, and have an \(L\)-Lipschitz gradient, without requiring convexity. A point \(x\) is first-order stationary when
\[\nabla f(x)=0,\]
and is \(\varepsilon\)-stationary when
\[\|\nabla f(x)\|\le\varepsilon.\]
Because stationarity need not imply global or local optimality, the canonical global performance criterion for a first-order algorithm is reduction of \(\min_{0\le k<K}\|\nabla f(x_k)\|\), rather than a guaranteed global objective gap.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Without convexity, smooth first-order analysis targets points with small gradient. Such stationarity does not by itself certify local or global optimality.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The regime uses \(\|\nabla f(x)\|\le\varepsilon\) as its standard approximate-solution criterion.

children.title: Smooth Convex Regime

knowledge_statements.title: Smooth Convex Regime
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Convex smooth minimization measured by global objective suboptimality.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The smooth convex regime consists of differentiable functions \(f:\mathbb{R}^d\to\mathbb{R}\) satisfying
\[f(y)\ge f(x)+\langle\nabla f(x),y-x\rangle\qquad\text{for all }x,y\in\mathbb{R}^d\]
and
\[\|\nabla f(x)-\nabla f(y)\|\le L\|x-y\|\qquad\text{for all }x,y\in\mathbb{R}^d.\]
When \(X^\star=\operatorname*{argmin}f\) is nonempty, the canonical accuracy criterion is the global gap \(f(x)-f^\star\le\varepsilon\), where \(f^\star=\min f\). Every stationary point is then a global minimizer.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Convexity turns first-order stationarity into global optimality. Algorithmic accuracy is naturally measured by objective value above the global minimum.
assumptions_latex: \(X^\star\ne\varnothing\) when an objective-gap criterion is invoked.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\nabla f(x)=0\) implies \(x\in X^\star\), and accuracy may be measured by \(f(x)-f^\star\le\varepsilon\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Gradient-descent objective-gap bound in the smooth convex regime
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Fixed-step gradient descent for unconstrained convex minimization with an L-Lipschitz gradient.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(f\in\mathcal F_L^{1,1}(\mathbb R^n)\), let \(x^*\in\operatorname*{argmin}f\), set \(f^*=f(x^*)\), and generate \(x_{k+1}=x_k-h\nabla f(x_k)\). If \(0<h<2/L\), then for every \(k\ge 0\),
\[
f(x_k)-f^*\leq \frac{2\bigl(f(x_0)-f^*\bigr)\|x_0-x^*\|^2}{2\|x_0-x^*\|^2+k h(2-Lh)\bigl(f(x_0)-f^*\bigr)}.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a convex function with L-Lipschitz gradient, fixed-step gradient descent with 0<h<2/L satisfies the displayed rational objective-gap bound.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: The explicit smooth-convex objective-gap rate obtained for the standard fixed step \(h=1/L\).

children.title: Smooth Strongly Convex Regime
children.top_down_role: Conditioned geometry supporting global contraction.

knowledge_statements.title: Smooth Strongly Convex Regime
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Smooth strongly convex minimization with finite condition number and unique minimizer.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The \((\mu,L)\)-smooth strongly convex regime consists of differentiable functions \(f:\mathbb{R}^d\to\mathbb{R}\) such that, for all \(x,y\in\mathbb{R}^d\),
\[f(y)\ge f(x)+\langle\nabla f(x),y-x\rangle+\frac{\mu}{2}\|y-x\|^2\]
and
\[\|\nabla f(x)-\nabla f(y)\|\le L\|x-y\|,\]
where \(0<\mu\le L\). Such an objective has at most one minimizer; when a minimizer \(x^\star\) exists, it is unique. The ratio \(\kappa=L/\mu\) is the condition number governing standard first-order contraction factors.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Strong convexity adds uniform positive curvature to smooth convexity, yielding a unique minimizer when attained and a finite condition number controlling first-order convergence.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The model is simultaneously \(\mu\)-strongly convex and \(L\)-smooth, with condition number \(\kappa=L/\mu\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Smooth and Strongly Convex Functions on a Hilbert Space
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Extraction-grounded definitions and equivalent characterizations used by the smooth strongly convex first-order regime.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(E\) be a real separable Hilbert space and let \(f:E\to\mathbb R\) be continuously differentiable. The function is \(L\)-smooth if \[\left|\left\langle f'(x)-f'(y),x-y\right\rangle\right|\le L\|x-y\|^2\qquad(x,y\in E),\] equivalently, \(\|f'(x)-f'(y)\|\le L\|x-y\|\). For \(l>0\) and \(Q\ge1\), it is \((l,Q)\)-strongly convex if \[l\|x-y\|^2\le\left\langle f'(x)-f'(y),x-y\right\rangle\le Ql\|x-y\|^2\qquad(x,y\in E).\] This is equivalent to \[f(x)+\langle f'(x),h\rangle+\frac l2\|h\|^2\le f(x+h)\le f(x)+\langle f'(x),h\rangle+\frac{Ql}{2}\|h\|^2\qquad(x,h\in E).\] If \(f\) is twice differentiable, the latter condition is equivalent to \(lI\preceq\nabla^2f(x)\preceq QlI\) for every \(x\), interpreted through spectral bounds in infinite dimension. For the optimal constants defined in the extract, \(Q_f=L_f/l_f\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An L-smooth function has an L-Lipschitz derivative. An (l,Q)-strongly convex function has derivative increments bounded below by l and above by Ql; equivalently, it admits matching lower and upper quadratic models. Twice differentiable functions satisfy the corresponding uniform Hessian spectral bounds.
assumptions_latex: E\text{ is a real separable Hilbert space}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: L\text{-smoothness is equivalent to }\operatorname{Lip}(f')\le L,\quad (l,Q)\text{-strong convexity is equivalent to the two-sided quadratic bounds, and for }f\in C^2,\ lI\preceq\nabla^2f(x)\preceq QlI.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Linear convergence of gradient descent in the smooth strongly convex regime
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Distance contraction for fixed-step gradient descent and the optimized-step distance and objective-gap bounds.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(f\in\mathcal S_{\mu,L}^{1,1}(\mathbb R^n)\), let \(x^*\) be its minimizer, set \(f^*=f(x^*)\), and generate \(x_{k+1}=x_k-h\nabla f(x_k)\). If \(0<h\leq 2/(\mu+L)\), then for every \(k\geq 0\),
\[
\|x_k-x^*\|^2\leq\left(1-\frac{2h\mu L}{\mu+L}\right)^k\|x_0-x^*\|^2.
\]
If \(h=2/(\mu+L)\) and \(Q_f=L/\mu\), then
\[
\|x_k-x^*\|\leq\left(\frac{Q_f-1}{Q_f+1}\right)^k\|x_0-x^*\|,
\]
\[
f(x_k)-f^*\leq\frac{L}{2}\left(\frac{Q_f-1}{Q_f+1}\right)^{2k}\|x_0-x^*\|^2.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a mu-strongly convex function with L-Lipschitz gradient, gradient descent contracts squared distance geometrically when 0<h<=2/(mu+L). At the endpoint step, the distance factor is (Q_f-1)/(Q_f+1), with the corresponding squared-factor objective-gap bound.

knowledge_statements.title: Polyak-Lojasiewicz Geometry
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Global Polyak–Łojasiewicz gradient dominance for a differentiable objective with an attained minimum.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}\) be differentiable, let \(f^*=\min_x f(x)\), and assume the minimum is attained. The function satisfies the Polyak–Łojasiewicz condition with constant \(\mu>0\) when
\[
\frac{1}{2}\lVert\nabla f(x)\rVert_2^2\geq \mu\bigl(f(x)-f^*\bigr)\qquad\text{for every }x\in\mathbb{R}^n.
\]
Consequently, every stationary point is globally minimizing, although the condition alone does not require \(f\) to be convex.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: PL geometry bounds objective suboptimality by the squared gradient norm, so every stationary point is a global minimizer without requiring convexity.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\frac12\lVert\nabla f(x)\rVert_2^2\geq\mu(f(x)-f^*)\) for all \(x\), hence \(\nabla f(x)=0\Rightarrow f(x)=f^*\).

knowledge_statements.title: Quadratic-Growth Geometry
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Global quadratic growth measured by Euclidean distance to the minimizer set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) have finite attained minimum \(f^*\), and write \(X^*=\operatorname*{argmin} f\neq\varnothing\). The function has quadratic growth with modulus \(\mu>0\) on a set \(D\subseteq\operatorname{dom}f\) when
\[
f(x)-f^*\geq \frac{\mu}{2}\operatorname{dist}(x,X^*)^2\qquad\text{for every }x\in D.
\]
Taking \(D=\operatorname{dom}f\) gives global quadratic growth; choosing a neighborhood of \(X^*\) gives the local form.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Quadratic growth lower-bounds objective error by a positive multiple of squared distance to the solution set.

notation.meaning: Euclidean distance from x to the minimizer set.

knowledge_statements.title: Residual Error-Bound Geometry
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Gradient-residual error bound for unconstrained differentiable minimization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}\) be differentiable with nonempty minimizer set \(X^*=\operatorname*{argmin}f\). A gradient-residual error bound holds on \(D\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) with constant \(\kappa>0\) when
\[
\operatorname{dist}(x,X^*)\leq \kappa\lVert\nabla f(x)\rVert_2\qquad\text{for every }x\in D.
\]
The condition is global when \(D=\mathbb{R}^n\), and local when \(D\) is a specified neighborhood or objective sublevel set containing \(X^*\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The gradient-residual error bound controls distance to the minimizer set by the gradient norm on a specified region.

notation.meaning: Region on which the error bound holds.

knowledge_statements.title: Growth–Error-Bound Equivalence Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Existential equivalence for convex differentiable objectives; constants need not be sharp.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}\) be convex and continuously differentiable, with nonempty closed minimizer set \(X^*\) and finite value \(f^*\). Suppose \(\nabla f\) is globally Lipschitz. Then the following global properties are equivalent: there exists \(\mu>0\) such that
\[
f(x)-f^*\geq\frac{\mu}{2}\operatorname{dist}(x,X^*)^2,
\]
and there exists \(\kappa>0\) such that
\[
\operatorname{dist}(x,X^*)\leq\kappa\lVert\nabla f(x)\rVert_2.
\]
Both inequalities are required for every \(x\in\mathbb{R}^n\); the analogous equivalence holds on compatible invariant sublevel regions under corresponding local hypotheses.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For convex smooth objectives, global quadratic growth is equivalent to a global gradient-residual error bound, up to changes in constants.
assumptions_latex: \(f\) is convex and continuously differentiable on \(\mathbb{R}^n\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\exists\mu>0\) satisfying quadratic growth if and only if \(\exists\kappa>0\) satisfying the gradient-residual error bound.
review_flags: exact equivalence hypotheses and localization regime require authoritative source confirmation

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The global equivalence is plausible under the stated convex smooth hypotheses, but its exact assumptions and constants require authoritative confirmation. The additional local-equivalence sentence does not specify the compatible regions, invariance requirement, or corresponding local hypotheses precisely enough to review independently.

knowledge_statements.title: Euclidean Gradient Geometry
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Riesz-gradient and steepest quadratic-model representation in finite-dimensional Euclidean space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For differentiable \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}\), the Euclidean gradient \(g=\nabla f(x)\) is the unique vector satisfying \(Df(x)[d]=\langle g,d\rangle_2\) for every direction \(d\). For any \(\alpha>0\), the Euclidean gradient step is equivalently characterized by
\[
d_x=\operatorname*{argmin}_{d\in\mathbb{R}^n}\left\{\langle g,d\rangle_2+\frac{1}{2\alpha}\lVert d\rVert_2^2\right\}=-\alpha g.
\]
Thus the gradient identifies the locally steepest direction under the Euclidean quadratic penalty.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The Euclidean gradient represents the derivative, and its negative scaled value uniquely minimizes the regularized local linear model.

notation.meaning: Directional action of the derivative at x on d.

knowledge_statements.title: Weighted Euclidean Geometry
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Fixed symmetric positive-definite metric and its preconditioned gradient representation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(M\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n}\) be symmetric positive definite. Define \(\langle u,v\rangle_M=u^{\mathsf T}Mv\), \(\lVert u\rVert_M=(u^{\mathsf T}Mu)^{1/2}\), and the dual norm \(\lVert g\rVert_{M^{-1}}=(g^{\mathsf T}M^{-1}g)^{1/2}\). For differentiable \(f\), its metric gradient is \(\operatorname{grad}_M f(x)=M^{-1}\nabla f(x)\), and
\[
\operatorname*{argmin}_{d}\left\{\langle\nabla f(x),d\rangle_2+\frac{1}{2\alpha}\lVert d\rVert_M^2\right\}=-\alpha M^{-1}\nabla f(x).
\]
Hence a fixed metric acts as a fixed preconditioner.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A positive-definite metric replaces the Euclidean gradient by the preconditioned vector obtained by applying the inverse metric matrix.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{grad}_M f(x)=M^{-1}\nabla f(x)\) and the metric step equals \(-\alpha M^{-1}\nabla f(x)\).

notation.meaning: Gradient relative to the M-inner product.

knowledge_statements.title: General-Norm Steepest Descent
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Steepest regularized direction under an arbitrary finite-dimensional norm and its dual.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(\lVert\cdot\rVert\) be a norm on \(\mathbb{R}^n\), with dual norm \(\lVert g\rVert_*\). Given \(g=\nabla f(x)\) and \(\alpha>0\), choose
\[
d_x\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{d\in\mathbb{R}^n}\left\{\langle g,d\rangle+\frac{1}{2\alpha}\lVert d\rVert^2\right\}.
\]
Every such direction satisfies \(\lVert d_x\rVert=\alpha\lVert g\rVert_*\), \(\langle g,d_x\rangle=-\alpha\lVert g\rVert_*^2\), and the minimum model value is \(-\alpha\lVert g\rVert_*^2/2\). The direction may be nonunique when the squared norm is not strictly convex.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: General-norm steepest descent minimizes a linearized objective plus squared norm penalty, with direction magnitude governed by the dual gradient norm.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(d_x\) minimizes the regularized linear model and satisfies \(\lVert d_x\rVert=\alpha\lVert\nabla f(x)\rVert_*\).

notation.meaning: Dual norm of the chosen primal norm.
Derivative represented in the standard dual pairing.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: The unit-sphere definition remains valid when the gradient vanishes. The unit-ball and unit-sphere argmin sets coincide when the gradient is nonzero; when it is zero, both have minimum value zero, but the ball formulation additionally admits nonunit minimizers.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For any norm, a normalized steepest descent direction is a unit vector producing the greatest decrease in the linear approximation of the objective. The minimum directional derivative equals minus the dual norm of the gradient. Scaling the normalized direction by that dual norm gives a steepest descent step whose inner product with the gradient is minus the squared dual norm. Equivalence of the unit-ball and unit-sphere minimizer sets requires a nonzero gradient.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Sublinear last-iterate objective bound for fixed-step gradient descent on smooth convex functions
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let f:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R} be convex and \beta-smooth with \beta>0, let x^*\in\operatorname*{argmin}f, and define x_{s+1}=x_s-\beta^{-1}\nabla f(x_s). Then, for every integer t\geq2, \[f(x_t)-f(x^*)\leq\frac{2\beta\lVert x_1-x^*\rVert^2}{t-1}.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For an unconstrained convex beta-smooth objective, gradient descent with fixed step size one over beta has a global deterministic last-iterate function-value bound of 2 beta times the squared initial distance divided by t minus one.
boundary_notes: The guarantee concerns function values at the last iterate, not convergence of the iterates themselves.
The supplied source does not state an epsilon-complexity theorem, so no complexity expression is materialized.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Input a differentiable objective \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}\), an initial point \(x_0\in\mathbb{R}^n\), positive stepsizes \((\alpha_k)_{k\geq0}\), and a stopping tolerance \(\varepsilon\geq0\). At iteration \(k\), evaluate \(g_k=\nabla f(x_k)\). If \(\lVert g_k\rVert_2\leq\varepsilon\), output \(x_k\); otherwise set
\[
x_{k+1}=x_k-\alpha_k g_k
\]
and continue. If no finite stopping time occurs, the output is the generated sequence \((x_k)_{k\geq0}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Gradient descent repeatedly subtracts a positive stepsize times the exact Euclidean gradient and stops when the gradient norm meets tolerance.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Best-iterate gradient bound for fixed-step gradient descent
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A finite-horizon gradient-norm guarantee for Euclidean gradient descent with stepsize $1/L$.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let $f\in\mathcal{F}_{1,L}^{1,1}(\mathbb{R}^n)$, let $x^*\in\arg\min f$, and set $R_0=\|x_0-x^*\|$. If $(x_k)_{k\ge0}$ is generated by the gradient method with constant stepsize $1/L$, then for every integer $T\ge3$ there exists $i\in\{0,\ldots,T\}$ such that $\|\nabla f(x_i)\|^2\le\frac{16L^2R_0^2}{(T+4)(T+6)}$. Equivalently, $\min_{0\le i\le T}\|\nabla f(x_i)\|\le\frac{4LR_0}{\sqrt{(T+4)(T+6)}}$.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For gradient descent with constant stepsize 1/L on the stated function class, every integer horizon of at least three contains an iterate satisfying the displayed gradient-norm bound.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: A finite-horizon stationarity guarantee for Euclidean gradient descent on an $L$-smooth convex objective.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let $f\in\mathcal{F}^{1,1}_L(\mathbb{R}^n)$, meaning that $f:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}$ is convex and continuously differentiable with $L$-Lipschitz continuous gradient. Let $x_*\in\arg\min f$, set $R_0=\|x_0-x_*\|$, and generate $x_{k+1}=x_k-L^{-1}\nabla f(x_k)$ for $k=0,\ldots,T-1$. Then, for every integer $T\ge3$, $g_{0,T}:=\min_{0\le k\le T}\|\nabla f(x_k)\|$ satisfies $g_{0,T}\le\frac{4LR_0}{\sqrt{(T+4)(T+6)}}$.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For an L-smooth convex objective with an attained minimum, gradient descent with stepsize 1/L attains the displayed gradient-norm bound among its first T plus one iterates for every integer T at least three.
assumptions_latex: f:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}\text{ is convex and continuously differentiable}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Objective-Gap Bound for Fixed-Step Gradient Descent
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Extraction-grounded finite-iterate bound for smooth convex gradient descent with a fixed step strictly between zero and \(2/L\); the zero-distance initialization is stated separately because the displayed source fraction becomes \(0/0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(f\in\mathcal F_L^{1,1}(\mathbb R^n)\) attain its minimum at \(x^*\), and set \(f^*=f(x^*)\). Let \(0<h<2/L\) and
\[
x_{k+1}=x_k-h\nabla f(x_k),\qquad k\ge0.
\]
If \(x_0\ne x^*\), then for every \(k\ge0\),
\[
f(x_k)-f^*\le
\frac{2\bigl(f(x_0)-f^*\bigr)\|x_0-x^*\|^2}
{2\|x_0-x^*\|^2+h(2-Lh)k\bigl(f(x_0)-f^*\bigr)}.
\]
If \(x_0=x^*\), then \(x_k=x^*\) and \(f(x_k)-f^*=0\) for every \(k\ge0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a convex differentiable function with L-Lipschitz gradient and an attained minimum, fixed-step gradient descent with 0<h<2/L obeys the stated rational objective-gap bound. Initialization at the chosen minimizer yields a stationary sequence with zero gap.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: x_0\ne x^*\Longrightarrow f(x_k)-f^*\le\frac{2(f(x_0)-f^*)\|x_0-x^*\|^2}{2\|x_0-x^*\|^2+h(2-Lh)k(f(x_0)-f^*)}\ \forall k\ge0;\qquad x_0=x^*\Longrightarrow x_k=x^*,\ f(x_k)-f^*=0\ \forall k\ge0

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Gradient descent can converge to a non-minimizing stationary point
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Smooth nonconvex counterexample. The invariant-line conclusion holds for arbitrary real steps, but convergence does not; a particular valid step choice establishes the claimed possibility.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let
\[
f(x^{(1)},x^{(2)})=\frac12(x^{(1)})^2+\frac14(x^{(2)})^4-\frac12(x^{(2)})^2.
\]
Its stationary points are $(0,0)$ and $(0,\pm1)$. The points $(0,\pm1)$ are isolated local minima, whereas $(0,0)$ is not a local minimum. For iterations
\[
x_{k+1}=x_k-h_k\nabla f(x_k),\qquad h_k\in\mathbb R,
\]
initialized at $x_0=(1,0)$, one has $x_k^{(2)}=0$ for every $k$. In particular, choosing $h_k=1$ gives $x_1=(0,0)$ and $x_k=(0,0)$ for all $k\ge1$, so gradient descent can converge to a non-minimizing stationary point. Invariance alone does not imply convergence for arbitrary real steps; for example, $h_k=0$ leaves $x_k=(1,0)$.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For the stated smooth quartic, (0,±1) are isolated local minima and (0,0) is stationary but not locally minimizing. Every gradient trajectory from (1,0) remains on the line with second coordinate zero. Unit steps reach (0,0), proving that gradient descent can converge to a non-minimizer. Arbitrary real steps do not all converge; zero steps provide an immediate failure case.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: x_k^{(2)}=0\ \forall k;\qquad h_k=1\ \forall k\implies x_k=(0,0)\ \forall k\ge1,\quad (0,0)\text{ is not a local minimizer}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Euclidean gradient descent update and output choices
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Basic Euclidean gradient descent for a differentiable convex objective, including its regularized first-order-model representation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f:\mathbb{R}^d\to\mathbb{R}\) be differentiable and convex, choose \(\eta>0\), and initialize \(\mathbf w^{(1)}\) (for example, \(\mathbf 0\)). At each iteration set \(\mathbf w^{(t+1)}=\mathbf w^{(t)}-\eta\nabla f(\mathbf w^{(t)})\). The same step is the unique minimizer of \[\frac12\|\mathbf w-\mathbf w^{(t)}\|^2+\eta\left(f(\mathbf w^{(t)})+\left\langle\mathbf w-\mathbf w^{(t)},\nabla f(\mathbf w^{(t)})\right\rangle\right).\] From the iterates \(\mathbf w^{(1)},\ldots,\mathbf w^{(T)}\), one may output their average \(\bar{\mathbf w}=T^{-1}\sum_{t=1}^T\mathbf w^{(t)}\), the last iterate, or an iterate attaining the smallest observed objective value.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Euclidean gradient descent subtracts a positive stepsize times the current gradient. Its step equivalently minimizes a squared-distance regularizer plus the objective's first-order model; the algorithm may return the averaged, last, or best observed iterate.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \mathbf w^{(t+1)}=\mathbf w^{(t)}-\eta\nabla f(\mathbf w^{(t)}),\qquad \bar{\mathbf w}=\frac1T\sum_{t=1}^T\mathbf w^{(t)}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Normalized negative-gradient direction and local descent
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines the normalized Euclidean negative-gradient direction and states its small-step descent property. The normalization is undefined when the gradient is zero, and the stated strict-improvement guarantee excludes that case.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: At iteration \(k\), set \(g^{(k)}=\nabla f(x^{(k)})\). If \(f\) is smooth and \(g^{(k)}\neq 0\), then the normalized steepest-descent direction is \(d^{(k)}=-g^{(k)}/\lVert g^{(k)}\rVert_2\), and sufficiently small positive steps along this direction decrease the objective: \(f(x^{(k)}+\alpha d^{(k)})<f(x^{(k)})\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At iteration k, the gradient is evaluated at the current point. For a smooth objective with nonzero gradient, the normalized Euclidean steepest-descent direction is the negative gradient divided by its norm, and every sufficiently small positive step along it strictly decreases the objective. The normalized direction is undefined at a zero-gradient point.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Input differentiable \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}\), \(x_0\in\mathbb{R}^n\), a fixed matrix \(M=M^{\mathsf T}\succ0\), positive stepsizes \((\alpha_k)\), and tolerance \(\varepsilon\geq0\). At iteration \(k\), compute \(g_k=\nabla f(x_k)\). If \(\lVert g_k\rVert_{M^{-1}}\leq\varepsilon\), output \(x_k\); otherwise compute the unique metric direction
\[
d_k=\operatorname*{argmin}_d\left\{\langle g_k,d\rangle_2+\frac12\lVert d\rVert_M^2\right\}=-M^{-1}g_k
\]
and update \(x_{k+1}=x_k+\alpha_k d_k\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Metric steepest descent applies the inverse fixed metric to the exact gradient before taking each prescribed step.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Linear-Change-of-Variables Representation of Scaled Steepest Descent
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Fixed positive-definite scaling as ordinary steepest descent in transformed coordinates, with the positive-definite variable-scaling extension and its stated limitation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let $f\in C^2(\mathbb R^n)$, let $T\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}$ be invertible, and define $x=Ty$ and $h(y)=f(Ty)$. Then steepest descent on $h$ transforms into
\[
x_{k+1}=x_k-\alpha_kD\nabla f(x_k),\qquad D=TT^{\mathsf T}\succ0,
\]
and
\[
\nabla^2h(y)=T^{\mathsf T}\nabla^2f(Ty)T.
\]
If $T$ is symmetric positive definite, then $T=D^{1/2}$ and the transformed Hessian is $D^{1/2}\nabla^2f(x)D^{1/2}$. Consequently, a positive-definite scaling approximating an inverse Hessian can improve conditioning. The iteration may be extended to $x_{k+1}=x_k-\alpha_kD_k\nabla f(x_k)$ with $D_k\succ0$; inverse-Hessian and diagonal inverse-curvature choices require positive definiteness, and simple diagonal scaling is not guaranteed to improve the convergence rate.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An invertible linear change of variables turns ordinary steepest descent into a gradient iteration with a symmetric positive-definite scaling matrix. The Hessian changes by congruence, so an inverse-Hessian-like positive-definite scaling can improve conditioning. Scaling may vary between iterations, but inverse-curvature choices must remain positive definite, and diagonal scaling is not guaranteed to improve convergence.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex:
y_{k+1}=y_k-\alpha_k
abla h(y_k)\implies x_{k+1}=x_k-\alpha_kD
abla f(x_k),\quad D=TT^{\mathsf T},\qquad 
abla^2h(y)=T^{\mathsf T}
abla^2f(Ty)T.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Euclidean steepest descent using a gradient-norm stopping test and exact minimization along each negative-gradient ray.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given $x_0\in\mathbb R^n$ and $\varepsilon>0$, set $k=0$. At iteration $k$, compute $g_k=\nabla f(x_k)$. If $\|g_k\|\le\varepsilon$, stop. Otherwise set $d_k=-g_k$, choose $\alpha_k\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{\alpha\ge0}f(x_k+\alpha d_k)$, set $x_{k+1}=x_k+\alpha_kd_k$, increment $k$, and repeat.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Starting from any point and a positive tolerance, stop when the gradient norm is at most the tolerance. Otherwise use the negative gradient as the direction, exactly minimize the objective over the nonnegative ray in that direction, update the iterate, and repeat.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Euclidean steepest-descent direction and gradient iteration
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The steepest-direction assertion is stated with the fixed-norm restriction required by the Cauchy–Schwarz argument; without such normalization, the directional derivative has no finite minimum.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let $f$ be continuously differentiable near $x_k$ and let $g_k=\nabla f(x_k)\ne0$. If $g_k^Td<0$, then $f(x_k+\alpha d)<f(x_k)$ for all sufficiently small $\alpha>0$. For every $\rho>0$, $\min_{\|d\|=\rho}g_k^Td=-\rho\|g_k\|$, attained uniquely at $d=-\rho g_k/\|g_k\|$. In particular, under the convention $\|d\|=\|g_k\|$, the steepest direction is $d_k=-g_k$, giving $x_{k+1}=x_k-\alpha_k g_k$.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a continuously differentiable objective with nonzero gradient, a direction having negative inner product with the gradient decreases the objective for every sufficiently small positive step. Among directions of a prescribed Euclidean norm, the negative-gradient direction uniquely minimizes the directional derivative. Choosing the direction as the negative gradient gives the standard gradient iteration.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: g_k^Td<0\Rightarrow f(x_k+\alpha d)<f(x_k)\text{ for all sufficiently small }\alpha>0;\quad \operatorname*{argmin}_{\|d\|=\rho}g_k^Td=\left\{-\rho\frac{g_k}{\|g_k\|}\right\},\quad x_{k+1}=x_k-\alpha_k g_k.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Linear Convergence Bounds for Exact-Line-Search Steepest Descent on a Positive-Definite Quadratic
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The exact-line-search qualification comes from the surrounding definition of the steepest-descent method. The displayed ratios apply when x_k\ne x^*; if x_k=x^*, the minimizer has already been reached. The Euclidean-norm factor need not be less than one for every condition number and therefore is recorded as a bound, not necessarily a per-step contraction.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let f(x)=\tfrac12x^TGx on \mathbb R^n, where G=G^T\succ0. Let \lambda_1=\lambda_{\max}(G), \lambda_n=\lambda_{\min}(G), \kappa=\lambda_1/\lambda_n, and \|v\|_G=(v^TGv)^{1/2}. If \{x_k\} is generated by Euclidean steepest descent with exact line search and x^* minimizes f, then x_k\to x^* at least linearly. For every k with x_k\ne x^*, \frac{f(x_{k+1})-f(x^*)}{f(x_k)-f(x^*)}\le\left(\frac{\kappa-1}{\kappa+1}\right)^2=\left(\frac{\lambda_1-\lambda_n}{\lambda_1+\lambda_n}\right)^2, \quad \frac{\|x_{k+1}-x^*\|_G}{\|x_k-x^*\|_G}\le\frac{\kappa-1}{\kappa+1}=\frac{\lambda_1-\lambda_n}{\lambda_1+\lambda_n}, \quad \frac{\|x_{k+1}-x^*\|}{\|x_k-x^*\|}\le\sqrt\kappa\,\frac{\kappa-1}{\kappa+1}=\sqrt{\frac{\lambda_1}{\lambda_n}}\frac{\lambda_1-\lambda_n}{\lambda_1+\lambda_n}.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Exact-line-search Euclidean steepest descent on a symmetric positive-definite quadratic converges linearly to its minimizer. The objective error and G-norm error satisfy the stated condition-number contraction bounds, while the Euclidean error satisfies the stated square-root-kappa bound.
assumptions_latex: \{x_k\}\text{ is generated by Euclidean steepest descent with exact line search}
x_k\ne x^*\text{ for the displayed ratios}

knowledge_statements.scope_note: The extract gives a qualitative mechanism for zigzagging and slowing. Its quantitative quadratic rate claim is reserved for the following theorem.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let f be differentiable at x_k, let g_k=\nabla f(x_k), and take the Euclidean steepest-descent direction d_k=-g_k. As \|\alpha d_k\|\to0, f(x_k+\alpha d_k)=f(x_k)-\alpha\|g_k\|^2+o(\|\alpha d_k\|). Thus the first-order decrease has magnitude \alpha\|g_k\|^2 and becomes small as the gradient becomes small. In the steepest-descent behavior described in the extract, orthogonality of successive gradients and directions produces zigzagging; for positive-definite quadratic objectives, more elongated contour ellipsoids correspond qualitatively to slower descent.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Along a Euclidean steepest-descent direction, the first-order objective change is minus the step length times the squared gradient norm, so this term becomes small near stationarity. Successive orthogonality explains zigzagging, and more elongated quadratic contours are associated with slower descent.

source_refs.locator: 8.1 From Gradient Descent to Subgradient Descent p. 195

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}\) have an \(L\)-Lipschitz gradient, and apply \(x_{k+1}=x_k-\alpha\nabla f(x_k)\) with a constant \(\alpha\in(0,2/L)\). Then the smoothness inequality gives
\[
f(x_{k+1})\leq f(x_k)-\alpha\left(1-\frac{L\alpha}{2}\right)\lVert\nabla f(x_k)\rVert_2^2.
\]
In particular, \(\alpha=1/L\) yields \(f(x_{k+1})\leq f(x_k)-\lVert\nabla f(x_k)\rVert_2^2/(2L)\). No convexity is required for this one-step descent guarantee.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Any constant step below twice the reciprocal smoothness yields objective descent; the standard reciprocal-smoothness step gives a simple gradient-square decrease.

knowledge_statements.title: Diminishing Stepsize Schedules
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Nonsummable diminishing schedules for smooth convex deterministic gradient descent.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A positive stepsize sequence \((\alpha_k)_{k\geq0}\) is a diminishing nonsummable schedule when
\[
\alpha_k>0,\qquad \alpha_k\to0,\qquad \sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\alpha_k=+\infty.
\]
For an \(L\)-smooth convex objective, a smooth deterministic specialization additionally imposes \(\alpha_k\leq1/L\). A standard polynomial family is \(\alpha_k=a/(k+b)^p\), where \(a>0\), \(b>0\), and \(0<p\leq1\), with \(a/b^p\leq1/L\). If square summability is also required, then \(p>1/2\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Diminishing schedules stay positive, converge to zero, and have divergent total length; polynomial schedules characterize when square summability also holds.
assumptions_latex: \(L>0\) when the smooth deterministic cap is imposed.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact-target Polyak steps for differentiable convex minimization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Input a differentiable convex objective \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}\), an initial point \(x_0\), and the known optimal value \(f^*=\min_x f(x)\). At iteration \(k\), compute \(g_k=\nabla f(x_k)\). If \(g_k=0\), output \(x_k\); otherwise set
\[
\alpha_k=\frac{f(x_k)-f^*}{\lVert g_k\rVert_2^2},
\qquad
x_{k+1}=x_k-\alpha_k g_k.
\]
The rule therefore requires an exact objective value and the target \(f^*\); replacing \(f^*\) by an estimate defines a different target-value policy.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The Polyak rule divides current objective error by squared gradient norm and therefore requires knowledge of the optimal target value.
knowledge_statements.title: Polyak Target-Value Stepsizes

knowledge_statements.title: Exact Line Search
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Unconstrained exact minimization along a fixed descent ray.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}\), let \(x_k\in\mathbb{R}^n\), and choose \(p_k\in\mathbb{R}^n\) with \(\nabla f(x_k)^\top p_k<0\). Define \(\phi_k(\alpha)=f(x_k+\alpha p_k)\) for \(\alpha\ge 0\). Exact line search selects any
\[
\alpha_k\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{\alpha\ge 0}\phi_k(\alpha)
\]
and outputs \(x_{k+1}=x_k+\alpha_kp_k\). The update is defined only when this argmin is nonempty. If \(\alpha_k>0\), \(f\) is differentiable, and \(\alpha_k\) is an interior minimizer, then \(\phi_k'(\alpha_k)=\nabla f(x_k+\alpha_kp_k)^\top p_k=0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Minimize the objective exactly along the chosen descent ray, then update by the minimizing step. Any interior minimizer makes the new gradient orthogonal to the search direction.
assumptions_latex: \(f\) is differentiable on an open set containing \(\{x_k+\alpha p_k:\alpha\ge0\}\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: General exact-line-search descent iteration
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A smooth unconstrained descent iteration using exact directional minimization and practical stopping tests.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given \(x^0\) and \(\varepsilon_1,\varepsilon_2,\varepsilon_3>0\), for \(i=1,2,\ldots\), choose \(u^i\) such that \(\nabla f(x^{i-1})^T u^i<0\), obtain \(\lambda_i\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{\lambda} f(x^{i-1}+\lambda u^i)\), and set \(x^i=x^{i-1}+\lambda_i u^i\). Stop if \(\|x^i-x^{i-1}\|<\varepsilon_1\), \(\|\nabla f(x^i)\|<\varepsilon_2\), or \(|f(x^i)-f(x^{i-1})|<\varepsilon_3\), and report \(x^*\approx x^i\). A prescribed combination of the tests, including conjunction, may replace the disjunction.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Starting from an initial point, repeatedly choose a descent direction, exactly minimize the objective along that direction, and update the iterate. Stop when the iterate change, gradient norm, or objective change satisfies its tolerance, unless a prescribed combination of these tests is required.
assumptions_latex: f:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}\text{ is differentiable at the iterates}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: x^i=x^{i-1}+\lambda_i u^i,\quad \text{with termination under the stated tolerance test and }x^*\approx x^i

knowledge_statements.scope_note: First-order necessary condition for a differentiable interior minimizer of the directional objective. The equality need not hold at a boundary minimizer.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\varphi(s)=F(x_k+s p)\) on a step domain \(\mathcal S\). If \(s^*\in\operatorname{int}(\mathcal S)\) minimizes \(\varphi\) and \(F\) is differentiable at \(x_k+s^*p\), then \(\varphi'(s^*)=p^T\nabla F(x_k+s^*p)=0\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Exact line-search rules on the directional objective
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The directional objective, the global-minimization and first-stationary-point rules called exact by the source, and the search-direction angle notation; stationarity alone is not asserted to imply global minimality.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Define $\phi(\alpha)=f(x_k+\alpha d_k)$ for $\alpha\geq0$. The global-minimization rule selects $\alpha_k\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{\alpha\geq0}\phi(\alpha)$ and hence $\phi(\alpha_k)\leq\phi(0)=f(x_k)$. The derivative-based rule called exact in the source selects the first nonnegative stationary point, $$\alpha_k=\min\{\alpha\geq0:
abla f(x_k+\alpha d_k)^Td_k=0\}.$$ These are distinct rules: without additional assumptions, the latter asserts stationarity rather than global minimality. For nonzero $d_k$ and $
abla f(x_k)$, $$\cos\angle(d_k,-
abla f(x_k))=- rac{d_k^T
abla f(x_k)}{\|d_k\|\,\|
abla f(x_k)\|}.$$
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The directional objective is phi(alpha)=f(x_k+alpha d_k). One rule globally minimizes phi over nonnegative alpha; another rule, also called exact in the source, selects its first nonnegative stationary point. The second rule guarantees only stationarity unless further conditions make that point a minimizer. The angle with the negative gradient is defined by the normalized negative directional derivative.
assumptions_latex: \{\alpha\geq0:\nabla f(x_k+\alpha d_k)^Td_k=0\}\text{ has a least element for the first-stationary-point rule}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex:
\phi(0)=f(x_k),\quad \phi(\alpha_k)\leq\phi(0)	ext{ for a global minimizer},\quad \alpha_k=\min\{\alpha\geq0:\phi'(\alpha)=0\}	ext{ for the first-stationary-point rule},\quad \cos\angle(d_k,-
abla f(x_k))=- rac{d_k^T
abla f(x_k)}{\|d_k\|\,\|
abla f(x_k)\|}.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Stationarity at a finite interior exact directional minimizer, together with existence and finite-implementation limitations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \phi(\alpha)=f(x^{(k)}+\alpha s^{(k)}). If f is differentiable along the search line and a finite interior exact minimizer \alpha^{(k)} of \phi exists, then \phi'(\alpha^{(k)})=0. Hence, with x^{(k+1)}=x^{(k)}+\alpha^{(k)}s^{(k)}, \nabla f(x^{(k+1)})^{T}s^{(k)}=0. A finite exact minimizer need not exist, and exact directional minimization is generally not finitely implementable; practical line searches therefore use prescribed approximate-minimum conditions.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At a finite interior exact line-search minimizer, the gradient at the new iterate is orthogonal to the search direction. A finite minimizer may not exist, and exact minimization generally cannot be implemented in finitely many operations, motivating inexact stopping conditions.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}\) and \(x,d\in\mathbb{R}^n\), define \(\varphi:\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}\) by \(\varphi(\tau)=f(x+\tau d)\). The exact line-search subproblem is \(\min_{\tau\in\mathbb{R}}\varphi(\tau)\). In an iterative minimization method, this scalar problem need not be solved exactly when an inexact step yields substantial improvement in the original objective.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A line search restricts the objective to the line through x in direction d. Exact line search minimizes this scalar function, but practical methods may instead accept an inexact step that substantially improves the objective.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{The exact directional subproblem is }\min_{\tau\in\mathbb{R}}\varphi(\tau),\text{ while exact solution is not required for every practical line search.}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Exact Line Search and the Quadratic Directional Step
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Covers only the exact directional-minimization portion owned by the existing node; the distinct Armijo backtracking material requires separate ownership.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given an iterate \(\theta_t\) and direction \(d_t\), exact line search chooses \(\eta_t\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{\eta>0}\mathcal L(\theta_t+\eta d_t)\). If \(\mathcal L\) is convex, then the restriction \(\phi_t(\eta)=\mathcal L(\theta_t+\eta d_t)\) is convex. For \(\mathcal L(\theta)=\frac12\theta^\top A\theta+b^\top\theta+c\), if \(d^\top A d>0\) and \(-d^\top(A\theta+b)/(d^\top A d)>0\), the exact minimizer over the positive ray is \(\eta=-\frac{d^\top(A\theta+b)}{d^\top A d}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Exact line search minimizes the objective along a positive search ray. A convex objective induces a convex one-dimensional restriction. For a quadratic with positive directional curvature, the displayed positive stationary step is the exact ray minimizer.
assumptions_latex: -\frac{d^\top(A\theta+b)}{d^\top A d}>0\text{ for an interior minimizer over the positive ray}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \eta_t\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{\eta>0}\mathcal L(\theta_t+\eta d_t);\quad \eta_t=-\frac{d^\top(A\theta+b)}{d^\top A d}\text{ in the stated quadratic interior case}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Exact line-search prescriptions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact directional minimization and the distinct stationary-root prescription on a nonnegative search ray.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given an iterate $x_k$ and direction $d_k$, one exact line-search prescription selects $\alpha_k\ge 0$ such that $$f(x_k+\alpha_k d_k)=\min_{\alpha\ge 0}f(x_k+\alpha d_k).$$ An alternative prescription, when the directional derivative exists and its nonnegative zero set has a least element, selects $$\alpha_k=\min\{\alpha\ge 0:\nabla f(x_k+\alpha d_k)^Td_k=0\}.$$
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An exact directional-minimization search chooses a global minimizer on the nonnegative ray. The source also gives a distinct prescription that chooses the smallest nonnegative stationary step when such a step exists.
assumptions_latex: \{\alpha\ge0:\nabla f(x_k+\alpha d_k)^Td_k=0\}\text{ has a least element for the stationary-root prescription}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Exact-line-search descent bound under strong gradient monotonicity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: One-step objective-decrease bound for an exact directional step. The extract does not specify the admissible step-size domain or separately state the sign of \eta.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \alpha_k be an exact step size for the search from x_k along d_k. Assume that f satisfies (x-z)^T[\nabla f(x)-\nabla f(z)]\ge \eta\|x-z\|^2 for all x,z covered by the hypothesis. Then f(x_k)-f(x_k+\alpha_k d_k)\ge \frac{1}{2}\eta\|\alpha_k d_k\|^2.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If alpha_k is an exact step size along d_k and the gradient satisfies the stated strong-monotonicity inequality with constant eta, then the objective decrease is at least one half eta times the squared norm of the accepted displacement.
assumptions_latex: \alpha_k\text{ is an exact step size for the search from }x_k\text{ along }d_k.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Exact line-search step for a convex quadratic
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Analytic minimization of a convex quadratic along a descent ray; the broader discussion of nonlinear bracketing and interpolation is not assigned to this narrower node.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(f(x)=\tfrac12x^TQx-b^Tx\), where \(Q=Q^T\succeq0\), and let \(\phi(\alpha)=f(x_k+\alpha p_k)\). If \(\nabla f(x_k)^Tp_k<0\) and \(p_k^TQp_k>0\), then the unique minimizer of \(\phi\) over \(\alpha\ge0\) is
\[
\alpha_k=-\frac{\nabla f(x_k)^Tp_k}{p_k^TQp_k}>0.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a convex quadratic, the exact minimizer along a descent ray is the negative directional derivative divided by the quadratic curvature, provided that curvature is positive.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Exact line search along a descent direction
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines exact directional minimization and identifies the derivative of the induced univariate objective when it exists.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given a point \(x\) and a descent direction \(d\), line search chooses a step factor by solving \(\operatorname*{minimize}_{\alpha} f(x+\alpha d)\). Writing \(\phi(\alpha)=f(x+\alpha d)\), if \(f\) is differentiable at \(x+\alpha d\), then \(\phi'(\alpha)=\nabla f(x+\alpha d)^{\mathsf T}d\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Given a point and a descent direction, exact line search minimizes the objective along the resulting line. Where the objective is differentiable, the derivative of the one-dimensional objective is its directional derivative along the search direction.

knowledge_statements.title: Interpolation Line Search
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Approximate directional minimization using safeguarded polynomial models.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\phi(\alpha)=f(x+\alpha p)\), and suppose values \(\phi(\alpha_i)\) and, when available, derivatives \(\phi'(\alpha_i)\) have been sampled. At each iteration construct a quadratic or cubic polynomial \(q\) interpolating the selected data. Compute a model minimizer \(\widehat\alpha\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{\alpha\in I}q(\alpha)\), then safeguard it by choosing \(\alpha^+\in I_{\mathrm{safe}}\subseteq I\), using \(\widehat\alpha\) when it lies in \(I_{\mathrm{safe}}\) and a prescribed fallback otherwise. Evaluate \(\phi(\alpha^+)\), update the sampled data and interval, and stop when the governing line-search acceptance condition holds; output \(\alpha^+\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Fit a quadratic or cubic model to sampled directional values or derivatives, safeguard its minimizer inside the admissible interval, and repeat until the chosen acceptance test holds.
assumptions_latex: \(f\) is differentiable along the sampled search line.
\(I_{\mathrm{safe}}\) is a nonempty prescribed subset of the current trial interval \(I\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The procedure outputs a safeguarded trial step satisfying the separately specified line-search acceptance condition.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Quadratic interpolation line search and safeguarding boundary
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Covers three-value quadratic interpolation, a derivative-assisted variant, and the absence of a general convergence guarantee for unsafeguarded interpolation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(\varphi\in C^2\) and suppose \(\alpha_k<\tau_k<\beta_k\) with \(\varphi(\alpha_k)>\varphi(\tau_k)<\varphi(\beta_k)\). The minimizer of the quadratic interpolant through these three values is
\[
\gamma_k=\frac{\varphi(\alpha_k)(\beta_k^2-\tau_k^2)+\varphi(\tau_k)(\alpha_k^2-\beta_k^2)+\varphi(\beta_k)(\tau_k^2-\alpha_k^2)}{2\left[\varphi(\alpha_k)(\beta_k-\tau_k)+\varphi(\tau_k)(\alpha_k-\beta_k)+\varphi(\beta_k)(\tau_k-\alpha_k)\right]}\in(\alpha_k,\beta_k).
\]
After evaluating \(\varphi(\gamma_k)\), discard an endpoint so that the best remaining point is the middle point. Without safeguards, convergence to a local minimizer is not generally guaranteed except under strong additional assumptions on \(\varphi''\); practical variants enforce sufficient bracket contraction. If \(\varphi'(0)<0\), \(\beta>0\), and \(\varphi(\beta)\geq\varphi(0)\), the quadratic interpolant determined by \(\varphi(0)\), \(\varphi'(0)\), and \(\varphi(\beta)\) has trial minimizer
\[
\tau=\frac{-\varphi'(0)\beta^2}{2[\varphi(\beta)-\varphi(0)-\varphi'(0)\beta]},\qquad 0<\tau\leq\frac{\beta}{2}.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Quadratic interpolation fits a parabola through a bracketing triple and evaluates its interior minimizer. The raw iteration lacks a general convergence guarantee, so practical versions safeguard bracket contraction. When the derivative at zero is known, two values and that derivative produce a trial point between zero and half the outer endpoint.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \gamma_k\in(\alpha_k,\beta_k),\quad\text{unsafeguarded interpolation has no general local-minimizer convergence guarantee, and in the derivative-assisted case }0<\tau\leq\beta/2.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Three-Point Quadratic Interpolation Formula
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The formula gives the stationary point of the quadratic interpolant. It gives a minimizing point only when the interpolant has positive quadratic coefficient.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Given three pairwise distinct points \(\alpha_1,\alpha_2,\alpha_3\) and values \(\phi_i=\phi(\alpha_i)\), there is a unique quadratic \(q(\alpha)=a\alpha^2+b\alpha+c\) satisfying \(q(\alpha_i)=\phi_i\) for \(i=1,2,3\). Define
\[
D=(\alpha_2-\alpha_3)\phi_1+(\alpha_3-\alpha_1)\phi_2+(\alpha_1-\alpha_2)\phi_3.
\]
If \(D\ne0\), equivalently \(a\ne0\), the stationary point is
\[
\bar\alpha=\frac12\frac{(\alpha_2^2-\alpha_3^2)\phi_1+(\alpha_3^2-\alpha_1^2)\phi_2+(\alpha_1^2-\alpha_2^2)\phi_3}{D}.
\]
The same formula follows by differentiating the three-point Lagrange interpolant and solving \(q'(\alpha)=0\). If \(a>0\), \(\bar\alpha\) minimizes \(q\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Three pairwise distinct function-value samples uniquely determine a quadratic interpolant. If its quadratic coefficient is nonzero, the displayed ratio gives its stationary point, equivalently the zero of the derivative of the three-point Lagrange interpolant. The stationary point is a minimizer only when the quadratic opens upward.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Two-Point Quadratic Interpolation from Two Values and One Derivative
knowledge_statements.scope_note: General univariate interpolation step. The displayed construction uses the derivative at the first point; the source also permits the symmetric construction using the derivative at the second point. The stationary point is a model minimizer only when the quadratic coefficient is positive.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Given distinct \(\alpha_1,\alpha_2\), values \(\phi_i=\phi(\alpha_i)\), and \(\phi'_1=\phi'(\alpha_1)\), construct the unique quadratic \(q(\alpha)=a\alpha^2+b\alpha+c\) satisfying \(q(\alpha_i)=\phi_i\) for \(i=1,2\) and \(q'(\alpha_1)=\phi'_1\). When \(a\ne0\), its stationary point is
\[
\bar\alpha=\alpha_1-\frac12\frac{(\alpha_1-\alpha_2)\phi'_1}{\phi'_1-(\phi_1-\phi_2)/(\alpha_1-\alpha_2)}.
\]
Accordingly, whenever the denominator is nonzero,
\[
\alpha_{k+1}=\alpha_k-\frac12\frac{(\alpha_k-\alpha_{k-1})\phi'_k}{\phi'_k-(\phi_k-\phi_{k-1})/(\alpha_k-\alpha_{k-1})}.
\]
After computing the trial point, compare it with the preceding points to reduce the bracket and continue until the bracket length is below the prescribed tolerance. The stationary point minimizes \(q\) when \(a>0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At two distinct points, interpolate both function values and one derivative by a quadratic. When the quadratic is nondegenerate, use its stationary point as the next trial point, reduce the bracket, and stop when the bracket is shorter than the prescribed tolerance. The stationary point is a minimizer only when the quadratic opens upward.
assumptions_latex: \text{A positive prescribed bracket-length tolerance is given.}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \bar\alpha=\alpha_1-\frac12\frac{(\alpha_1-\alpha_2)\phi'_1}{\phi'_1-(\phi_1-\phi_2)/(\alpha_1-\alpha_2)},\qquad \text{followed by bracket reduction until the tolerance is met.}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Safeguarded quadratic-interpolation trial update
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Quadratic interpolation for choosing a reduced trial after rejection in an inexact line search.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(\phi(\alpha)=f(x_k+\alpha d_k)\). The quadratic interpolant matching \(\phi(0)\), \(\phi'(0)=\nabla f(x_k)^Td_k\), and \(\phi(1)\) is
\[
m(\alpha)=[\phi(1)-\phi(0)-\phi'(0)]\alpha^2+\phi'(0)\alpha+\phi(0).
\]
If the unit trial is rejected and \(\phi(1)-\phi(0)-\phi'(0)\ne0\), the stationary point
\[
\widehat\alpha=-\frac{\phi'(0)}{2[\phi(1)-\phi(0)-\phi'(0)]}
\]
may be used as the next trial value. Separately, for a prescribed least step \(\mathrm{minstep}\), a rejected trial terminates the line search when \(\|\alpha_kd_k\|<\mathrm{minstep}\). The extract does not guarantee that \(\widehat\alpha\) is positive, minimizing, or acceptable, so further safeguards may be required.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Fit a quadratic through the objective value and directional derivative at zero and the objective value at the unit trial. If the unit trial is rejected and the formula is defined, its stationary point may be tried next. A rejected trial whose displacement is below the prescribed minimum step terminates the search; the interpolation formula alone does not guarantee a positive or acceptable step.
assumptions_latex: The unit trial fails the prescribed line-search acceptance condition before the interpolation update is used.
A least-step threshold \(\mathrm{minstep}\) is prescribed for the stopping safeguard.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\widehat\alpha\) is an optional next trial value; if a rejected trial satisfies \(\|\alpha_kd_k\|<\mathrm{minstep}\), the line search stops.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Safeguarded quadratic and cubic interpolation line search
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Interpolation-based search for a step satisfying sufficient decrease, with safeguards on successive trial reductions and an alternative Hermite-cubic variant when trial derivatives are inexpensive.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Assume \(\phi'(0)<0\), \(0<c_1<1\), and \(\alpha_0>0\). Accept a trial \(\alpha_i\) when
\[
\phi(\alpha_i)\leq \phi(0)+c_1\alpha_i\phi'(0).
\]
If \(\alpha_0\) fails this test, minimize the quadratic interpolating \(\phi(0)\), \(\phi'(0)\), and \(\phi(\alpha_0)\), obtaining
\[
\alpha_1=-\frac{\phi'(0)\alpha_0^2}{2\bigl(\phi(\alpha_0)-\phi(0)-\alpha_0\phi'(0)\bigr)}.
\]
After a further failure, form a cubic interpolating \(\phi(0)\), \(\phi'(0)\), and the two most recent function values, and use its minimizing trial. Repeat until the sufficient-decrease test is met. If a proposed trial is too close to, or excessively smaller than, its predecessor, replace it by \(\alpha_i=\alpha_{i-1}/2\). When derivatives at trial points are inexpensive, one may instead minimize within the current bracket the Hermite cubic interpolating \(\phi\) and \(\phi'\) at the two most recent trials.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Test the initial step for sufficient decrease. After failure, try the minimizer of a quadratic interpolant and then minimizers of cubic interpolants based on the latest data. Replace an unsafe reduction by half the preceding trial. If trial derivatives are inexpensive, a cubic matching both values and derivatives at the two latest trials can be used instead.
assumptions_latex: \phi\text{ and, for the Hermite variant, }\phi'\text{ are available at the required trial points}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Secant Formula from Two-Point Derivative Interpolation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The function value determines the constant term of the quadratic, whereas its stationary point depends only on the two derivative samples. The update is undefined when those derivative samples coincide.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Given distinct \(\alpha_1,\alpha_2\), one value \(\phi(\alpha_1)\), and derivatives \(\phi'_i=\phi'(\alpha_i)\), construct \(q(\alpha)=a\alpha^2+b\alpha+c\) so that \(q(\alpha_1)=\phi(\alpha_1)\) and \(q'(\alpha_i)=\phi'_i\) for \(i=1,2\). If \(\phi'_1\ne\phi'_2\), its stationary point is
\[
\bar\alpha=\alpha_1-\frac{\alpha_1-\alpha_2}{\phi'_1-\phi'_2}\phi'_1.
\]
Consequently,
\[
\alpha_{k+1}=\alpha_k-\frac{\alpha_k-\alpha_{k-1}}{\phi'_k-\phi'_{k-1}}\phi'_k.
\]
Equivalently, \(\alpha_{k+1}\) is the zero of the affine Lagrange interpolant of \(\phi'\) through the two derivative samples.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Interpolate two derivative samples by an affine function, equivalently constructing a quadratic that also matches one function value. When the sampled derivatives differ, the zero of the derivative interpolant gives the secant update.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \alpha_{k+1}=\alpha_k-\frac{\alpha_k-\alpha_{k-1}}{\phi'(\alpha_k)-\phi'(\alpha_{k-1})}\phi'(\alpha_k),\qquad \text{the zero of the affine interpolant of }\phi'.

knowledge_statements.title: Armijo Backtracking
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Geometric backtracking until Armijo sufficient decrease holds.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Given \(x_k\in\mathbb{R}^n\), a direction \(p_k\) satisfying \(g_k^\top p_k<0\), parameters \(c\in(0,1)\), \(\rho\in(0,1)\), and an initial trial \(\bar\alpha>0\), initialize \(\alpha\leftarrow\bar\alpha\). While
\[
f(x_k+\alpha p_k)>f(x_k)+c\alpha g_k^\top p_k,
\]
replace \(\alpha\leftarrow\rho\alpha\). On termination set \(\alpha_k=\alpha\) and output \(x_{k+1}=x_k+\alpha_kp_k\). If \(f\) is continuously differentiable near \(x_k\), the loop terminates after finitely many reductions.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Repeatedly shrink an initial positive step by a fixed factor until the objective achieves Armijo sufficient decrease, then accept the resulting iterate.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A finite backtracking index \(j\ge0\) exists with \(\alpha_k=\bar\alpha\rho^j\) satisfying \(f(x_k+\alpha_kp_k)\le f(x_k)+c\alpha_kg_k^\top p_k\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Armijo geometric backtracking rule
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Geometric trial-step selection by the first Armijo sufficient-decrease test, conditional on finite acceptance.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given $\beta\in(0,1)$, $\rho\in(0,\tfrac12)$, $\tau>0$, and $g_k=\nabla f(x_k)$, define $$M_k=\left\{m\in\mathbb{Z}_{\ge0}:f(x_k)-f(x_k+\beta^m\tau d_k)\ge-\rho\beta^m\tau g_k^Td_k\right\}.$$ If $M_k\ne\varnothing$, choose $m_k=\min M_k$ and the trial step $\alpha_k=\beta^{m_k}\tau$.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Starting from tau, contract the trial step geometrically by beta and accept the first Armijo-sufficient step, provided such a trial occurs.

knowledge_statements.title: Goldstein Search
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Classical two-sided sufficient-decrease condition for a descent direction.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}\) be differentiable, let \(x_k,p_k\in\mathbb{R}^n\), and suppose \(g_k^\top p_k<0\), where \(g_k=\nabla f(x_k)\). For a parameter \(c\in(0,\tfrac12)\), a step \(\alpha_k>0\) satisfies the Goldstein conditions when
\[
f(x_k)+(1-c)\alpha_k g_k^\top p_k
\le f(x_k+\alpha_kp_k)
\le f(x_k)+c\alpha_k g_k^\top p_k.
\]
The right inequality requires sufficient decrease, while the left inequality excludes steps whose decrease is excessively large relative to the first-order model, thereby preventing an unnecessarily short accepted step.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Accept a positive step only when its objective value lies between two affine bounds based on the initial directional derivative.
assumptions_latex: \(f\) is differentiable along \(x_k+\alpha p_k\) for relevant \(\alpha\ge0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\alpha_k\) is Goldstein-acceptable exactly when the displayed two-sided inequalities hold.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Goldstein acceptable-step conditions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Two-sided function-value acceptance along a differentiable descent ray; no general existence or interval-shape theorem is asserted.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let $g_k=\nabla f(x_k)$, let $g_k^Td_k<0$, and let $0<\rho<\tfrac12$. A positive step $\alpha$ is Goldstein-acceptable when $$f(x_k+\alpha d_k)\le f(x_k)+\rho\alpha g_k^Td_k$$ and $$f(x_k+\alpha d_k)\ge f(x_k)+(1-\rho)\alpha g_k^Td_k.$$ In a setting where all acceptable steps form an interval $[b,c]$, that set is called the acceptable interval.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The Goldstein rule accepts a positive step whose objective value lies between two affine bounds based on the initial directional derivative. When the acceptable set is an interval, it is called the acceptable interval.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: f(x_k)+(1-\rho)\alpha g_k^Td_k\le f(x_k+\alpha d_k)\le f(x_k)+\rho\alpha g_k^Td_k

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Goldstein lower bound may exclude an exact line minimizer
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure boundary for the lower function-value inequality in two-sided Goldstein acceptance.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let $\phi(\alpha)=f(x_k+\alpha d_k)$, let $0<\rho<\tfrac12$, and suppose a positive exact line minimizer exists. It is possible that some $$\alpha_*\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{\alpha\ge0}\phi(\alpha)$$ fails the Goldstein lower inequality, namely, $$\phi(\alpha_*)<\phi(0)+(1-\rho)\alpha_*\phi'(0).$$ Such an exact minimizer is then excluded from the Goldstein acceptable set.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The Goldstein lower bound can reject a positive step that globally minimizes the objective along the search ray.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Bracket-and-Expand Goldstein Line Search
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Algorithmic statement only; the extract asserts neither termination nor convergence.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Choose \(\rho\in(0,\tfrac12)\), \(t>1\), and \(\alpha_0\in[0,+\infty)\), or use a bounded interval \([0,\alpha_{\max}]\). Set \(a_0=0\), \(b_0=+\infty\), or \(b_0=\alpha_{\max}\) in the bounded case. At iteration \(k\), if \(\phi(\alpha_k)>\phi(0)+\rho\alpha_k\phi'(0)\), set \((a_{k+1},b_{k+1})=(a_k,\alpha_k)\) and choose the next trial by bisection. Otherwise, stop if \(\phi(\alpha_k)\geq\phi(0)+(1-\rho)\alpha_k\phi'(0)\). If this second inequality fails, set \((a_{k+1},b_{k+1})=(\alpha_k,b_k)\); bisect when \(b_{k+1}<+\infty\), and otherwise set \(\alpha_{k+1}=t\alpha_k\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Maintain lower and upper trial-step bounds. Failure of the upper Goldstein inequality lowers the upper bound. Failure of the lower Goldstein inequality raises the lower bound. Bisect a finite bracket or expand an unbounded trial by the factor t, and stop only when both inequalities hold.
assumptions_latex: \phi(0),\ \phi'(0),\ \text{and each required trial value }\phi(\alpha_k)\text{ are evaluable}
